summary: First empirical study of GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw), where developers write a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter (triggers, permissions, engine, tools, 'safe-outputs' limits) that compiles to a GitHub Actions workflow, and a Markdown body of natural-language instructions the agent interprets at run time. The corpus is 1,248 gh-aw files from 276 repositories with at least 10 stars, plus 7,446 commits and 20,841 changes. RQ1 describes the files (median 556.5 body words, code blocks in 62.1%, Flesch reading ease 38.8; 29.6% of projects import Markdown from another repository). RQ2 tracks 348 files in 43 projects over four months: churn falls and maintenance touches frontmatter more often than bodies. RQ3 hand-labels 288 bodies with an instruction taxonomy (pre-resolution kappa=0.61). Task, output, constraint and process instructions are near-universal; resource budgets appear in 38.2% and prompt-injection defences in 9.4%. RQ4 finds Gemini 3.1 Pro labels instructions at F1 0.818. Descriptive study with a public replication package; no outcome or effectiveness data.

claims.claim: Developers specify how agents should work, not only what to do: process instructions appear in 93.4% of bodies, including required sequences (88.2%) and decision branches (87.2%)
claims.evidence: 288 hand-labelled files; two annotators, kappa=0.61 before resolution, with one label at kappa=0.238 (145 vs 81 assignments). Work delegation appears in only 9.0%.

claims.claim: Few workflows include prompt-injection defences (9.4%) or resource budgets (38.2%)
claims.evidence: Counts come from body-only coding (§III-D excludes YAML frontmatter and imports), so platform-level controls such as safe-outputs limits, permissions and the gh-aw firewall are not counted. The figure measures prose mentions, not actual exposure.

claims.claim: Maintenance concentrates early and more often touches frontmatter than the instruction body
claims.evidence: 348 files in 43 projects: 78.2% updated in month 4 (read from a figure); median churn 31.2 -> 5.6 (p=.011); project-level median 74.5% of changes touch frontmatter vs 50.0% the body. The tracked set is files that survived, a selection effect the authors acknowledge.

claims.claim: gh-aw files are long, structured documents reused across repositories
claims.evidence: Median 556.5 body words and 58 frontmatter lines; code blocks in 62.1%; 108 of 365 projects (29.6%) reference Markdown from another repository. The corpus includes many github/* and githubnext/* files.

claims.claim: LLMs can assign instruction labels reliably
claims.evidence: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview F1 0.818, kappa 0.715 against resolved human labels at T=0; GLM-5.2 and GPT-OSS-120B lower. Single run per configuration, scored against the same 288 files used to build the taxonomy.

patterns.note: gh-aw is a hybrid: a static outer shell (trigger, permissions, safe-outputs, tool allow-lists compiled to a GitHub Actions job) wrapping steps the agent interprets from prose. Required sequences (88.2%) and decision branches (87.2%) are written as natural language, not as graph edges. The paper's implication (§V-A) is to move firm limits into frontmatter, e.g. safe-outputs add-comment max 1, rather than prose. Adoption evidence only; no comparison of enforced vs prose-specified flow.
9.4% of bodies mention injection defences, but platform controls in frontmatter were excluded from coding, so true exposure is unknown.
Recommends enforcing limits through frontmatter configuration over body instructions; no measurement of compliance or violations.
Resource budgets stated in 38.2% of bodies; frontmatter-level limits not counted.
29.6% of projects import Markdown instructions from another repository: cross-repo instruction reuse is real practice.
Workflow Markdown functions as an executable task spec for recurring automation; studied descriptively.
Instruction files persist across runs; no memory mechanism is evaluated.
Work delegation appears in only 9.0% of bodies, so multi-agent hand-offs are rare in practice.

[retag 2026-10-08] RQ3 taxonomy (288 hand-labelled gh-aw bodies): Domain Context (subject knowledge, business rules, API conventions, protocols) appears in 34.0% and Repository Context in 70.1%. Both are written as prose inside the workflow instructions, not as machine-readable artifacts. Domain Context is also the label the LLM labeller gets most wrong (kappa 0.414, 83 false positives, Table V). Descriptive only; no outcome data.

methodology.sample: 1,248 gh-aw files from 276 repositories (>=10 stars); 7,446 commits / 20,841 changes; RQ2 subset 348 files / 43 projects over four months; RQ3 288 labelled files
methodology.baselines: None (descriptive); RQ4 compares three labelling LLMs against human labels
methodology.models: RQ4: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, GLM-5.2, GPT-OSS-120B via Vertex AI at T=0
methodology.variance: Single labelling run per model and prompt; Wilcoxon-type test for churn
methodology.languages: Markdown/YAML workflow files across mixed-language repositories

standards.artifacts: Replication package with dataset, scripts and labelling material (github.com/stilab-ets/ghaw)

biases.detail: RQ2 tracks files that persisted for four months; abandoned workflows are excluded.
Security and budget prevalence is measured in prose bodies while frontmatter controls are excluded, which understates actual safeguards.
Many examples come from github/*, githubnext/* and gh-aw's own repositories, which may reflect the platform team's style rather than typical adopters.
No link from instruction style to workflow success, failure or incidents.

coi.affiliations: École de technologie supérieure (ÉTS); Université Laval
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GitHub Agentic Workflows (studied descriptively); Gemini and others for labelling
coi.detail: Academic authors; Google compute credits; Gemini is the best labeller, which is a minor and incidental tie. No product is promoted.

verdict_reason: A careful, reproducible descriptive study of a new agent-workflow format with a released dataset and agreement statistics. The caveats are that it measures what developers write, not whether it works, and the security and budget prevalence figures ignore frontmatter controls by design.
applicability: Directly relevant if the team runs agents in CI. Practice converges on a deterministic outer shell (trigger, permissions, output caps compiled to Actions) with the step order left as prose for the agent. That is a cheap middle ground between a full static graph and an open loop. The concrete takeaway: put hard limits (number of comments or PRs, write scopes, budgets) in machine-enforced config rather than instructions, and treat sequencing in prose as advisory. Cross-repo imports (29.6% of projects) also support keeping shared workflow instructions in one repository that the 4+ ingestion repos reference. The study does not show whether enforcing the sequence as a graph would improve outcomes.

conflicts_with.detail: Agree in direction: many security rules written in CLAUDE.md prose have a matching deterministic Claude Code control that would enforce them, consistent with this paper's advice to move limits from Markdown bodies into gh-aw frontmatter.

Complementary: in GitHub Actions agent workflows, edges passing free-form agent output to later deterministic steps are the main injection channel (84.5%). The 9.4% prose-defence rate here says little about that channel because frontmatter safe-outputs were not coded.
